harder.updated_question: Common challenges of AI in aviation
harder.verification_criterion: The answer lists at least three specific challenges that AI systems face when implemented in aviation contexts (e.g., safety certification, data quality, explainability, regulatory compliance, edge cases, sensor reliability, etc.)

attempts.answer:
Below is a concise synthesis of the common challenges of applying AI in aviation, organized by technical, operational, regulatory, and human factors themes, with evidence from recent surveys, certification analyses, and domain studies.

Summary
Across aviation applications, the most salient barriers are aligning probabilistic ML with rigorous safety certification and explainability requirements, managing complex, heterogeneous, and streaming operational data, ensuring trustworthy human–automation interaction, and integrating AI safely into legacy and cyber‑physical constraints while meeting privacy and cybersecurity obligations over the product lifecycle. <cite id="b7545b6c-0">Certification challenges persist due to the fundamentally probabilistic nature of AI and difficulty fitting these systems into traditional rule-based regulatory frameworks, alongside concerns about data integrity, bias, cybersecurity, and maintaining pilot situational awareness in increasingly automated cockpits</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-1">Regulators have begun formalizing strategies for safe integration, with FAA and EASA AI roadmaps outlining phased, risk‑based assurance pathways</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-4">Standards must expand to address AI’s probabilistic behavior, identify new failure causes, and become more agile to support iterative updates</cite>.

1) Safety assurance, certification, and explainability
Aviation safety cultures demand proof of safety and understandability, but many AI methods are probabilistic, adaptive, and opaque, creating friction with deterministic certification norms. <cite id="b7545b6c-0">Improving AI transparency and explainability is crucial to build trust among regulators and operators, and ensuring consistent safety assurance as AI systems learn and evolve remains an open area; integrating autonomous systems into existing ATM and preserving pilot situational awareness are ongoing hurdles</cite>. <cite id="b7545b6c-2">FAA-certifiable systems face intertwined operational, explainability, and certification considerations; aligning these within a single framework strengthens the link between technical performance and regulatory acceptability</cite>. <cite id="b7545b6c-3">FAA’s AI Safety Assurance Roadmap promotes an incremental, risk-based strategy, distinguishes learned (evolving) from static AI, and highlights certification gaps for evolving AI, bias mitigation, and comprehensive guidelines for autonomous systems; ethical considerations and public trust are underexplored</cite>. <cite id="b7545b6c-4">Current certification standards need to incorporate ML-specific methods for specification, traceability, and verification, and to accommodate accelerating ML hardware; agile, iterative certification is needed for continuous safety assurance</cite>.

2) Data, models, and generalization: quality, scale, and streaming evidence
Aviation data are high-dimensional, heterogeneous, multimodal, and temporally complex, and they grow as fleets and sensors expand. <cite id="dd016634-0">Detecting anomalies in aviation is challenging due to large volume, high dimensionality, heterogeneity (mixed categorical/continuous), multi-modality (aircraft, airports, airspace), and temporality; growth in air traffic and sensorized systems will make this harder</cite> <cite id="dd016634-1">Distance-based methods are computationally expensive and unsuitable for real-time; probabilistic, domain-based, and reconstruction-based methods train slowly but test quickly, creating a gap for online safety monitoring that needs incremental or fast online learning</cite>. Labeling is often impractical, pushing toward unsupervised and weakly supervised methods. <cite id="dd016634-2">Supervised approaches perform well but require massive effort to label aviation data, which is largely impractical; a CVAE-based unsupervised approach improved over classic and deep-learning baselines on time-series anomalies, yielding higher precision and recall</cite>. Operational realities split use cases between offline post‑operational analysis and online safety monitoring. <cite id="dd016634-1">Most aviation anomaly applications are offline post‑operational rather than online real-time, despite the need for fast detection for safety</cite> <cite id="dd016634-4">Exceedance-based rule thresholds struggle with new risks and nonlinear, multiscale relationships in multivariate, multimodal flight and environmental data; ML methods (e.g., clustering, autoencoders) are increasingly investigated to capture such complexity</cite>. Coverage remains uneven across subdomains. <cite id="dd016634-3">Anomaly detection is most mature in safety and maintenance; underrepresented areas include environmental monitoring and pilot performance, with future opportunities in urban air mobility and autonomous aviation</cite>.

3) Human–automation interaction: trust, complacency, and out‑of‑the‑loop risks
Even with capability gains, over‑reliance and degraded situational awareness are persistent hazards. <cite id="da1d8a99-0">Automation complacency is a long‑recognized causal factor in aviation accidents; more than half of surveyed airline captains cited it as the leading cause; empirical work links complacency to sub‑optimal monitoring frequency and degraded performance, with vigilance defined as the lack of complacency</cite> <cite id="da1d8a99-1">Preliminary experiments show half of subjects failed to recognize subtle automation failure, consistent with aviation accident reviews highlighting ineffective monitoring and degraded SA</cite>. Design choices can skew trust and attention in ways that harm safety. <cite id="da1d8a99-3">Studies report that high pilot trust correlates with low monitoring; over‑trust led to failures to cancel insignificant diversion aids, especially when information quality was low, with negative performance effects</cite>. Single‑pilot operations surface additional constraints. <cite id="da1d8a99-2">Automation can exhibit brittleness (good within design scope but needing human intervention outside), create out‑of‑the‑loop syndrome, and interact with authority gradients; designers must determine automation extent, when to use aids, and conditions under which they may be unused</cite>. These dynamics complicate certification and operation of AI in cockpits. <cite id="b7545b6c-0">Ensuring pilots remain situationally aware in increasingly automated cockpits is an ongoing hurdle</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-4">Existing certification focuses too heavily on pilot support and explainability for some applications, revealing missing technological methods and critical defeaters in OP arguments</cite>.

4) Cyber‑physical constraints, standards, and real‑time inference
Airborne AI must meet stringent reliability, latency, and hardware constraints while remaining certifiable. <cite id="b7545b6c-4">Standards must identify new failure causes for ML (e.g., overfitting, data shift), assess applicability of traditional architectural mechanisms to ML, integrate ML‑specific specification, traceability, and verification methods, and accommodate ML‑accelerating hardware; certification processes must become agile to support iterative updates</cite>. Certification roadmaps reflect these tensions and call for incremental deployment. <cite id="b7545b6c-3">The FAA roadmap distinguishes static pretrained models (learned AI) from adaptive, evolving systems (learning AI), noting that the latter pose significant certification challenges due to unpredictability, limited explainability, and potential bias, underscoring the need for standardized assurance protocols</cite>. Operational monitoring methods also expose practical bottlenecks. <cite id="dd016634-1">Distance-based anomaly detectors are quadratic in training size, unsuitable for very large datasets and some applications; although reconstruction-based deep methods work well offline, they may be hard to apply online without incremental or very fast training</cite>.

5) Cybersecurity, privacy, and data governance
AI systems depend on continuous, high‑quality data flows and must withstand adversarial threats and privacy constraints. <cite id="b7545b6c-0">Concerns about data integrity, bias, and cybersecurity pose risks that must be carefully managed</cite>. Certification and assurance frameworks increasingly embed these concerns. <cite id="b7545b6c-2">Certifiable aviation AI must account for bias and explainability alongside operational performance</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-3">Robust bias mitigation and regulatory guidelines for autonomous AI systems are lacking, indicating ethical and trust gaps that must be addressed</cite>. Across anomaly detection and cyber‑physical monitoring, data come from diverse, sensitive sources. <cite id="dd016634-3">Primary sources include sensor data and control logs (safety), maintenance logs and predictive models (maintenance), flight phase and pilot action logs (performance), and communication/trajectory data (ATC), highlighting the breadth of data types and the need for secure, compliant handling</cite>.

6) Interoperability and integration with air traffic management and legacy systems
Scaling AI into the broader aviation ecosystem requires compatibility with existing ATC, avionics, and fleet heterogeneity. <cite id="b7545b6c-0">Integrating autonomous systems with existing air traffic management remains a hurdle, and ensuring pilots’ situational awareness amid higher automation levels is difficult</cite>. Standards and roadmaps seek to bridge domains. <cite id="b7545b6c-1">EASA’s AI Roadmap 2.0 and FAA’s AI Safety Assurance Roadmap provide high‑level pathways and guiding principles to assure safety of AI in aircraft design and operation, complemented by technical interchange meetings to build safety evidence and operational confidence</cite>. Knowledge transfer and data scarcity complicate deployment across fleets. <cite id="b7545b6c-4">Validating knowledge transfer in the face of data limitations is a key research need; specifying intended behavior for validation and improving verification (especially testing sufficiency) are also required</cite>.

7) Lifecycle governance: training, culture, and continuous assurance
AI’s behavior can evolve in service, demanding ongoing monitoring, update assurance, and workforce readiness. <cite id="b7545b6c-4">The certification process must become more agile, supporting iterative updates to ensure continuous safety assurance; developing training methods and architectures that prioritize safety over performance is needed</cite>. Human factors and organizational change are as important as algorithms. <cite id="da1d8a99-2">Designers should avoid misuse, disuse, and overreliance, and address cognitive overheads that can outweigh benefits; for single‑pilot operations, determining the extent of automation and conditions for non‑use is critical</cite>. Cross‑stakeholder coordination is essential. <cite id="b7545b6c-1">Regulators, manufacturers, operators, and standards bodies collaborate in TIs and forums to share evidence and refine safety methodologies, enabling responsible, risk‑informed adoption</cite>.

8) Representative application pain points: air traffic and autonomous operations
In anomaly detection for safety and maintenance, data complexity and streaming constraints are acute. <cite id="dd016634-0">Multi‑modal, long‑time‑series aviation data complicate detection of operationally significant events</cite> <cite id="dd016634-2">Unsupervised deep generative models can improve detection without expert labels, addressing labeling cost and improving recall/precision versus baselines</cite>. For single‑pilot and advanced autonomy, trust calibration and robustness to out‑of‑distribution events are critical. <cite id="da1d8a99-2">Automation brittleness and out‑of‑the‑loop risks require careful design of automation control modes and attention to authority gradients</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-4">Evolving AI raises certification issues around unpredictability and bias that current methods struggle to address</cite>. Emerging domains like urban air mobility heighten these challenges. <cite id="dd016634-3">Future applications in complex, data‑rich environments such as urban air mobility and autonomous aviation systems are expected to expand the role of ML, but also to surface new integration and assurance needs</cite>.

Practical mitigation directions
- Build explainability by design and align with certification concepts. <cite id="b7545b6c-2">Integrating operational, explainability, and certification considerations strengthens regulatory acceptability</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-3">Neurosymbolic approaches can improve interpretability and support certifiable frameworks, while highlighting gaps in bias mitigation and standardized assurance</cite>.
- Tame data complexity with hybrid pipelines. <cite id="dd016634-1">Use probabilistic/reconstruction-based methods for offline training and fast inference, complemented by lightweight online or incremental learning where feasible</cite> <cite id="dd016634-2">Adopt unsupervised/weakly supervised methods to reduce labeling costs while improving anomaly detection performance</cite>.
- Human-in-the-loop with calibrated trust. <cite id="da1d8a99-0">Account for complacency by enforcing optimal monitoring cadence and vigilance cues</cite> <cite id="da1d8a99-3">Design for trust calibration and quality‑aware decision aids to prevent over‑reliance in degraded information conditions</cite>.
- Engineer to standards with agile assurance. <cite id="b7545b6c-4">Augment standards with ML-specific failure models, traceability, and verification methods, and adopt agile, iterative certification to keep pace with updates</cite>.
- Secure the data pipeline and governance. <cite id="b7545b6c-0">Mitigate risks around data integrity, bias, and cybersecurity</cite> <cite id="dd016634-3">Implement robust access, privacy, and integrity controls across heterogeneous sources used for safety, maintenance, pilot performance, and ATC</cite>.
- Integrate into legacy/ATM safely. <cite id="b7545b6c-0">Use phased, risk‑based deployment and pilot‑aware design to preserve situational awareness</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-1">Leverage regulator–industry roadmaps and collaborative forums to build safety evidence and operational confidence</cite>.

What remains uncertain or contested
Some challenges have emergent, unsettled science. <cite id="da1d8a99-0">Complacency is widely cited in accident reports and operator surveys, yet its definition, mechanisms, and remedies remain debated, with calls for more empirical foundations</cite>. Certification and assurance for evolving/learning AI still lack mature, universally accepted methods. <cite id="b7545b6c-3">Roadmaps identify gaps in robust certification for evolving AI, bias mitigation, and comprehensive guidelines for autonomous systems</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-4">Further research is needed on specifying intended behavior, sufficiency of testing, and validating knowledge transfer under data limitations</cite>. More empirical evidence linking specific AI architectures and deployment patterns to measurable safety outcomes across operational domains would help resolve these gaps.

Bottom line
AI in aviation is constrained by a tight coupling of probabilistic models with safety‑critical, human‑centered, and cyber‑physical environments. Progress hinges on explainable, certifiable AI; data‑efficient, robust learning pipelines for complex, streaming aviation data; trustworthy human–automation partnerships; secure, compliant data governance; and phased integration into legacy and ATC systems with agile, lifecycle safety assurance. <cite id="b7545b6c-0">These challenges are recognized by regulators and operators, who emphasize explainability, evolving safety assurance, data integrity and cybersecurity, pilot awareness, and integration hurdles</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-1">and are being addressed through coordinated regulatory roadmaps and collaborative assurance practices</cite> <cite id="b7545b6c-4">with calls for standards and processes that accommodate ML’s probabilistic behavior and accelerating hardware while enabling iterative, safe updates</cite>.

Title: Recent Advances in Anomaly Detection Methods Applied to Aviation
Snippet: In this survey, we have reviewed the state-of-the-art in data-driven anomaly detection and its application to the aviation domain. Thus, we have introduced a large number of classical and more recent approaches and described how some of them have been applied to areas such as air traffic operations and predictive maintenance. Machine learning models can work with offline or online data to detect significant events for further analysis by aviation experts as part of decision support or condition monitoring tools. The ultimate goal of the presented applications is to help improve the performance of ATM and maintenance operations, in particular safety. 

In general, as stated by Janakiraman and Nielsen [56], the data-driven detection of anomalies in aviation data is particularly challenging because of its large volume, high-dimensionality, heterogeneity (mixed categorical and continuous attributes), multi-modality (multiple modes of nominal and non-nominal operations with different types of aircraft, airports and airspaces) and temporality (long time-series). The challenge is expected to be even bigger in the future because of the forecast world-wide growth of air traffic and the ever higher number of sensor-equipped aviation systems and operational complexity. 

Classical nearest-neighbour and clustering-based approaches do not scale well with such massive amounts of high-dimensional data. In the case of high-dimensional data, the use of a dimensionality reduction technique as a preprocessing step (e.g., to clustering) or the application of a reconstruction-based method is often a better solution. On the other hand, distance-based methods are computationally expensive when applied to large volumes of data, even during the test phase, which makes them unsuitable for real-time applications. However, in the case of probabilistic, domain-based and reconstruction-based methods, even though the training phase can be time-consuming, the test phase is very efficient. This is not an issue for applications where models can be trained offline, but some real-time safety monitoring applications may require some kind of incremental or very fast online training. 

In aviation, among the traditional approaches, the domain-based MKAD [44] developed by NASA is still one of the state-of-the-art methods for the detection of operationally significant events in flight data.
</snippet>
<snippet id=dd016634-1>
Title: Recent Advances in Anomaly Detection Methods Applied to Aviation
Snippet: In aviation, among the traditional approaches, the domain-based MKAD [44] developed by NASA is still one of the state-of-the-art methods for the detection of operationally significant events in flight data. However, its computational complexity is quadratic with respect to the number of training examples, which makes it unsuitable for very large datasets and certain applications. ClusterAD methods are also among the most widely applied, in spite of having the same performance issues than MKAD. For faster learning with large datasets, ELM [56] or LoOP [16] based anomaly detection seem to be two good alternatives to MKAD. 

The recent advances in anomaly detection we have covered in this review are mainly based on techniques developed in the field of neural networks and deep learning. In principle, deep-learning approaches should be better adapted than traditional machine learning methods [11] when it comes to find anomalies in large-scale high-complex data as the one generally available in aviation. We have also reviewed the advances in temporal-logic based learning as an alternative approach that should help the user more naturally understand and trust the results expressed in terms of logical formulae. 

The application area related to the identification of significant events in air traffic operations is particularly rich in terms of the number and variety of the anomaly methods applied. While traditional techniques are widely used, there exists also some attempts to apply recent advances in temporal-logic learning [103,111], RNN [58] and advanced autoencoders (e.g., ConvLSTM-AE [86]). The vast majority of the research in this application area concern the detection of anomalies relevant to safety, although we provided also a few examples of anomalies related to potential cyberattacks or air traffic congestion. Another observation is that most of the introduced applications work in an offline configuration with post-operational data for analysis purposes rather than with online data to support real-time monitoring tasks. 

As for the other application area concerning predictive maintenance in aviation, we have reviewed a few anomaly detection methods aimed at identifying incipient failures in aviation system components from flight and maintenance data. These data-driven methods play an increasingly important role in PHM which is necessary to achieve true condition-based maintenance.
</snippet>

Title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Flight Data Using Convolutional Variational Auto-Encoder
Snippet: In order to improve and automate identification of unknown vulnerabilities in flight operations, we have developed an unsupervised machine learning approach for identifying operationally significant anomalies in high-dimensional heterogeneous aviation time-series. The proposed approach constructs models based on observed operations and identifies operationally significant safety anomalies. This algorithm is demonstrated to have improved performance as compared to existing anomaly detection methods used in the aviation domain. This translates to increased visibility of previously undetected vulnerabilities that if gone unmonitored and unaddressed may lead to a more serious incident or accident. The majority of approaches presented in the aerospace literature either rely on rule-based thresholding or supervised learning approaches. Although the supervised approaches show a good performance, creating labels for aviation data requires a huge amount of effort and is largely impractical. Our approach builds upon recent advancements in deep generative models to develop the Convolutional Variational Auto-Encoder (CVAE), which is an unsupervised approach for anomaly detection in high-dimensional heterogeneous time-series data (Figure 1). It is important to note that there is a significant cost to missing each unknown incident and any improvement upon the detection rates helps to increase awareness and consequently safety. Having an unsupervised method that does not require valuable subject matter expert's feedback can assist in this process and is a key aspect of being proactive to reduce incident and accident levels in anticipation of growing air traffic demands in the future. 

We validate CVAE in relation to several classic approaches (e.g., KMeans clustering and one-class support vector machines) as well as deep learning-based approaches (e.g., autoencoder, generative adversarial networks), used in the literature for anomaly detection in various data sets. Validating CVAE on Yahoo!'s benchmark time series anomaly detection database, we show that our model outperforms both classic approaches (∼48 pp higher precision, and ∼29 pp higher recall) and deep learning based approaches (on average ∼44 pp higher precision and ∼60 pp higher recall) (Figure 3).
</snippet>

Title: Anomaly Detection for Aviation Cyber-Physical System: Opportunities and Challenges
Snippet: • In the safety sector, the primary data sources include sensor data (e.g., flight sensors, environmental sensors) and control system logs, which are essential for detecting deviations that could lead to safety risks. 

• For maintenance, the data primarily consists of historical maintenance logs, real-time sensor data, and predictive maintenance models that analyze trends to forecast potential equipment failures. 

• In flight phases and pilot performance, flight data recordings and pilot action logs are utilized to monitor and detect anomalies in specific flight phases, which are critical for preventing in-flight incidents. 

• In air traffic control, the focus is on communication logs and flight trajectory data used to monitor and ensure the safety and efficiency of air traffic management. The Figure 10 visually summarizes the distribution of anomaly detection applications across these sectors, reinforcing the textual analysis. 

The diversity of sectors in which anomaly detection techniques are applied underscores these models' broad applicability and necessity across Aviation CPS. snippet.text: The FAA Roadmap for AI Safety Assurance1 establishes a structured, phased approach for integrating artificial intelligence into aviation, a domain traditionally governed by deterministic safety protocols. The roadmap advocates for an incremental, risk-based strategy, initially focusing on low-criticality systems to gather operational data and refine safety assurance processes before transitioning to highstakes, safety-critical applications. This iterative engineering approach ensures that early-stage insights inform the deployment of more complex AI-driven systems. A key aspect of the roadmap is its distinction between learned AI (static, pretrained models) and learning AI (adaptive, real-time evolving systems). While learning AI enhances adaptability and responsiveness, it poses significant certification challenges due to its inherent unpredictability, limited explainability, and potential for bias issues that conventional safety methodologies struggle to address. The roadmap underscores the importance of regulatory alignment with existing aviation safety frameworks, advocating for industry collaboration among regulatory bodies, government agencies, and stakeholders to establish standardized AI assurance protocols. However, it highlights critical gaps, including the lack of robust certification methods for evolving AI, inadequate bias mitigation strategies, and the absence of comprehensive regulatory guidelines for autonomous AIdriven aviation systems. Ethical considerations, essential for public trust and system accountability, receive minimal focus, indicating an area requiring further exploration. Addressing these challenges is essential for ensuring safe, reliable AI integration into aviation while maintaining compliance with rigorous industry standards. By integrating Neurosymbolic AI, the FAA can establish a robust, certifiable AI framework that enhances aviation safety while accelerating the adoption of AI in autonomous flight operations.

snippet.text:
The integration of AI in aerospace offers significant potential but requires rigorous attention to safety and certification. Our literature review highlights AI's pivotal role in predictive maintenance, anomaly detection, engine health monitoring, fuel consumption optimization, avoidance, aircraft trajectory prediction, and autonomous flight operations. We complex AI methods in high-criticality systems and simpler AI methods in low-criticality systems. 

To advance the certification of AI-enabled aviation systems, we assessed existing aviation certification standards and examined their applicability to ML technologies. Current standards must expand to address AI's unique challenges, especially its probabilistic behavior. 

Standards must identify new failure causes, assess the applicability of architectural mechanisms to ML, integrate ML-specific methods for specification, traceability, and verification, and accommodate MLaccelerating hardware. Furthermore, the certification process must become more agile, supporting iterative updates to ensure continuous safety assurance. 

We applied current certification efforts for certifying MLaviation systems, such as EASA concept paper 2.0 and Overarching Properties (OPs), to ADIMA, an AI-enabled peripherical detection system used for DAL A to D systems. Although we found alignment with several objectives, the concept paper focuses too heavily on pilot support, emphasizing explainability and human factors, which is not relevant or applicable for all applications. The created OP argument revealed critical defeaters due to missing technological methods. 

Drawing from our experience applying certification efforts and analysis of ML technology, we identified the need for further research in critical areas: specifying intended behavior for validation, improving verification methods (particularly testing sufficiency), developing training methods and model architectures that prioritize safety over performance, and validating knowledge transfer in the face of data limitations. 

Future work should focus on creating adaptive standards and developing inherently safer, more transparent ML methods.

Title: Recent Advances in Anomaly Detection Methods Applied to Aviation
Snippet: In this survey, we have reviewed the state-of-the-art in data-driven anomaly detection and its application to the aviation domain. Thus, we have introduced a large number of classical and more recent approaches and described how some of them have been applied to areas such as air traffic operations and predictive maintenance. Machine learning models can work with offline or online data to detect significant events for further analysis by aviation experts as part of decision support or condition monitoring tools. The ultimate goal of the presented applications is to help improve the performance of ATM and maintenance operations, in particular safety. 

In general, as stated by Janakiraman and Nielsen [56], the data-driven detection of anomalies in aviation data is particularly challenging because of its large volume, high-dimensionality, heterogeneity (mixed categorical and continuous attributes), multi-modality (multiple modes of nominal and non-nominal operations with different types of aircraft, airports and airspaces) and temporality (long time-series). The challenge is expected to be even bigger in the future because of the forecast world-wide growth of air traffic and the ever higher number of sensor-equipped aviation systems and operational complexity. 

Classical nearest-neighbour and clustering-based approaches do not scale well with such massive amounts of high-dimensional data. In the case of high-dimensional data, the use of a dimensionality reduction technique as a preprocessing step (e.g., to clustering) or the application of a reconstruction-based method is often a better solution. On the other hand, distance-based methods are computationally expensive when applied to large volumes of data, even during the test phase, which makes them unsuitable for real-time applications. However, in the case of probabilistic, domain-based and reconstruction-based methods, even though the training phase can be time-consuming, the test phase is very efficient. This is not an issue for applications where models can be trained offline, but some real-time safety monitoring applications may require some kind of incremental or very fast online training. 

In aviation, among the traditional approaches, the domain-based MKAD [44] developed by NASA is still one of the state-of-the-art methods for the detection of operationally significant events in flight data.

Title: Recent Advances in Anomaly Detection Methods Applied to Aviation
Snippet: In aviation, among the traditional approaches, the domain-based MKAD [44] developed by NASA is still one of the state-of-the-art methods for the detection of operationally significant events in flight data. However, its computational complexity is quadratic with respect to the number of training examples, which makes it unsuitable for very large datasets and certain applications. ClusterAD methods are also among the most widely applied, in spite of having the same performance issues than MKAD. For faster learning with large datasets, ELM [56] or LoOP [16] based anomaly detection seem to be two good alternatives to MKAD. 

The recent advances in anomaly detection we have covered in this review are mainly based on techniques developed in the field of neural networks and deep learning. In principle, deep-learning approaches should be better adapted than traditional machine learning methods [11] when it comes to find anomalies in large-scale high-complex data as the one generally available in aviation. We have also reviewed the advances in temporal-logic based learning as an alternative approach that should help the user more naturally understand and trust the results expressed in terms of logical formulae. 

The application area related to the identification of significant events in air traffic operations is particularly rich in terms of the number and variety of the anomaly methods applied. While traditional techniques are widely used, there exists also some attempts to apply recent advances in temporal-logic learning [103,111], RNN [58] and advanced autoencoders (e.g., ConvLSTM-AE [86]). The vast majority of the research in this application area concern the detection of anomalies relevant to safety, although we provided also a few examples of anomalies related to potential cyberattacks or air traffic congestion. Another observation is that most of the introduced applications work in an offline configuration with post-operational data for analysis purposes rather than with online data to support real-time monitoring tasks. 

As for the other application area concerning predictive maintenance in aviation, we have reviewed a few anomaly detection methods aimed at identifying incipient failures in aviation system components from flight and maintenance data. These data-driven methods play an increasingly important role in PHM which is necessary to achieve true condition-based maintenance.

Title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Flight Data Using Convolutional Variational Auto-Encoder
Snippet: In order to improve and automate identification of unknown vulnerabilities in flight operations, we have developed an unsupervised machine learning approach for identifying operationally significant anomalies in high-dimensional heterogeneous aviation time-series. The proposed approach constructs models based on observed operations and identifies operationally significant safety anomalies. This algorithm is demonstrated to have improved performance as compared to existing anomaly detection methods used in the aviation domain. This translates to increased visibility of previously undetected vulnerabilities that if gone unmonitored and unaddressed may lead to a more serious incident or accident. The majority of approaches presented in the aerospace literature either rely on rule-based thresholding or supervised learning approaches. Although the supervised approaches show a good performance, creating labels for aviation data requires a huge amount of effort and is largely impractical. Our approach builds upon recent advancements in deep generative models to develop the Convolutional Variational Auto-Encoder (CVAE), which is an unsupervised approach for anomaly detection in high-dimensional heterogeneous time-series data (Figure 1). It is important to note that there is a significant cost to missing each unknown incident and any improvement upon the detection rates helps to increase awareness and consequently safety. Having an unsupervised method that does not require valuable subject matter expert's feedback can assist in this process and is a key aspect of being proactive to reduce incident and accident levels in anticipation of growing air traffic demands in the future. 

We validate CVAE in relation to several classic approaches (e.g., KMeans clustering and one-class support vector machines) as well as deep learning-based approaches (e.g., autoencoder, generative adversarial networks), used in the literature for anomaly detection in various data sets. Validating CVAE on Yahoo!'s benchmark time series anomaly detection database, we show that our model outperforms both classic approaches (∼48 pp higher precision, and ∼29 pp higher recall) and deep learning based approaches (on average ∼44 pp higher precision and ∼60 pp higher recall) (Figure 3).

Title: Anomaly Detection for Aviation Cyber-Physical System: Opportunities and Challenges
Snippet: • In the safety sector, the primary data sources include sensor data (e.g., flight sensors, environmental sensors) and control system logs, which are essential for detecting deviations that could lead to safety risks. 

• For maintenance, the data primarily consists of historical maintenance logs, real-time sensor data, and predictive maintenance models that analyze trends to forecast potential equipment failures. 

• In flight phases and pilot performance, flight data recordings and pilot action logs are utilized to monitor and detect anomalies in specific flight phases, which are critical for preventing in-flight incidents. 

• In air traffic control, the focus is on communication logs and flight trajectory data used to monitor and ensure the safety and efficiency of air traffic management. The Figure 10 visually summarizes the distribution of anomaly detection applications across these sectors, reinforcing the textual analysis. 

The diversity of sectors in which anomaly detection techniques are applied underscores these models' broad applicability and necessity across Aviation CPS. However, the concentration in specific areas like safety and maintenance suggests that these sectors are where anomaly detection can have the most immediate and significant impact shown in Figure 10. The findings indicate that while anomaly detection is becoming more integrated into various aspects of aviation operations, there remains a need for further development and refinement in underrepresented areas, such as pilot performance monitoring and environmental anomaly detection. 

While the primary focus is on safety and maintenance, sectors like environmental monitoring and pilot performance have seen less application of anomaly detection techniques. Future research could explore these areas further, mainly as new challenges such as climate change introduce new variables to aviation safety. The ongoing integration of machine learning and AI into anomaly detection in Aviation CPS suggests potential future applications in more complex and data-rich environments, such as urban air mobility and autonomous aviation systems.

Title: On the Exploration of Temporal Fusion Transformers for Anomaly Detection with Multivariate Aviation Time-Series Data
Snippet: In the last two decades, safety risk management in civil aviation has shifted from postaccident investigations and analyses to proactively identifying emerging safety hazards and incorporating the analyses of these proactive findings to supplement post-accident investigations. This type of shift requires applying new approaches that can process a large amount of multivariate time-series aviation data from various data sources that can be both time-varying and categorical. Identifying anomalous events within historical flight data is crucial for the extraction of various safety hazards. These hazards can be associated with various factors, including adverse weather conditions (such as heavy rain and strong winds), mechanical failures, human error (pilot, air traffic controller), airspace congestion, inadequate flight planning, ground operations, difficult terrain, and bird strikes, among others. The standard anomaly detection technique applied to aviation data is to use exceedance detection methods [1]. These methods require domain knowledge and involve comparing specific flight parameters with respect to aircraft-dependent thresholds pre-defined by aviation subject matter experts. Because exceedance-based methods are based on rules with strict thresholds [2], they face limitations when identifying new safety risks and capturing useful information from the acquired multivariate and multimodal flight and environmental data with complex and nonlinear relationships that take place at different temporal scales. Recently, machine learning techniques have been used to fill this emergent gap, and they have been investigated for their potential to automatically identify anomalies in multivariate flight data. 

Exploring machine learning techniques to be used with flight sensor data for improving aviation safety is an active research field. Li et al. [3] introduced a cluster-based anomaly detection approach to detect abnormal flights, which can support domain experts in detecting anomalies and associated risks from routine airline operations. Their and determine the precursors to the predicted adverse events. Recently, an autoencoder architecture has been used for anomaly detection with time-series flight sensor data, which utilizes the reconstruction error as the anomaly score [17,18]. Variational autoencoders (VAE) have also been investigated for their potential in anomaly detection [1].

documents.title: Recent Advances in Anomaly Detection Methods Applied to Aviation
documents.snippet:
In this survey, we have reviewed the state-of-the-art in data-driven anomaly detection and its application to the aviation domain. Thus, we have introduced a large number of classical and more recent approaches and described how some of them have been applied to areas such as air traffic operations and predictive maintenance. Machine learning models can work with offline or online data to detect significant events for further analysis by aviation experts as part of decision support or condition monitoring tools. The ultimate goal of the presented applications is to help improve the performance of ATM and maintenance operations, in particular safety. 

In general, as stated by Janakiraman and Nielsen [56], the data-driven detection of anomalies in aviation data is particularly challenging because of its large volume, high-dimensionality, heterogeneity (mixed categorical and continuous attributes), multi-modality (multiple modes of nominal and non-nominal operations with different types of aircraft, airports and airspaces) and temporality (long time-series). The challenge is expected to be even bigger in the future because of the forecast world-wide growth of air traffic and the ever higher number of sensor-equipped aviation systems and operational complexity. 

Classical nearest-neighbour and clustering-based approaches do not scale well with such massive amounts of high-dimensional data. In the case of high-dimensional data, the use of a dimensionality reduction technique as a preprocessing step (e.g., to clustering) or the application of a reconstruction-based method is often a better solution. On the other hand, distance-based methods are computationally expensive when applied to large volumes of data, even during the test phase, which makes them unsuitable for real-time applications. However, in the case of probabilistic, domain-based and reconstruction-based methods, even though the training phase can be time-consuming, the test phase is very efficient. This is not an issue for applications where models can be trained offline, but some real-time safety monitoring applications may require some kind of incremental or very fast online training. 

In aviation, among the traditional approaches, the domain-based MKAD [44] developed by NASA is still one of the state-of-the-art methods for the detection of operationally significant events in flight data.

In aviation, among the traditional approaches, the domain-based MKAD [44] developed by NASA is still one of the state-of-the-art methods for the detection of operationally significant events in flight data. However, its computational complexity is quadratic with respect to the number of training examples, which makes it unsuitable for very large datasets and certain applications. ClusterAD methods are also among the most widely applied, in spite of having the same performance issues than MKAD. For faster learning with large datasets, ELM [56] or LoOP [16] based anomaly detection seem to be two good alternatives to MKAD. 

The recent advances in anomaly detection we have covered in this review are mainly based on techniques developed in the field of neural networks and deep learning. In principle, deep-learning approaches should be better adapted than traditional machine learning methods [11] when it comes to find anomalies in large-scale high-complex data as the one generally available in aviation. We have also reviewed the advances in temporal-logic based learning as an alternative approach that should help the user more naturally understand and trust the results expressed in terms of logical formulae. 

The application area related to the identification of significant events in air traffic operations is particularly rich in terms of the number and variety of the anomaly methods applied. While traditional techniques are widely used, there exists also some attempts to apply recent advances in temporal-logic learning [103,111], RNN [58] and advanced autoencoders (e.g., ConvLSTM-AE [86]). The vast majority of the research in this application area concern the detection of anomalies relevant to safety, although we provided also a few examples of anomalies related to potential cyberattacks or air traffic congestion. Another observation is that most of the introduced applications work in an offline configuration with post-operational data for analysis purposes rather than with online data to support real-time monitoring tasks. 

As for the other application area concerning predictive maintenance in aviation, we have reviewed a few anomaly detection methods aimed at identifying incipient failures in aviation system components from flight and maintenance data. These data-driven methods play an increasingly important role in PHM which is necessary to achieve true condition-based maintenance.

documents.title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Flight Data Using Convolutional Variational Auto-Encoder
documents.snippet:
In order to improve and automate identification of unknown vulnerabilities in flight operations, we have developed an unsupervised machine learning approach for identifying operationally significant anomalies in high-dimensional heterogeneous aviation time-series. The proposed approach constructs models based on observed operations and identifies operationally significant safety anomalies. This algorithm is demonstrated to have improved performance as compared to existing anomaly detection methods used in the aviation domain. This translates to increased visibility of previously undetected vulnerabilities that if gone unmonitored and unaddressed may lead to a more serious incident or accident. The majority of approaches presented in the aerospace literature either rely on rule-based thresholding or supervised learning approaches. Although the supervised approaches show a good performance, creating labels for aviation data requires a huge amount of effort and is largely impractical. Our approach builds upon recent advancements in deep generative models to develop the Convolutional Variational Auto-Encoder (CVAE), which is an unsupervised approach for anomaly detection in high-dimensional heterogeneous time-series data (Figure 1). It is important to note that there is a significant cost to missing each unknown incident and any improvement upon the detection rates helps to increase awareness and consequently safety. Having an unsupervised method that does not require valuable subject matter expert's feedback can assist in this process and is a key aspect of being proactive to reduce incident and accident levels in anticipation of growing air traffic demands in the future. 

We validate CVAE in relation to several classic approaches (e.g., KMeans clustering and one-class support vector machines) as well as deep learning-based approaches (e.g., autoencoder, generative adversarial networks), used in the literature for anomaly detection in various data sets. Validating CVAE on Yahoo!'s benchmark time series anomaly detection database, we show that our model outperforms both classic approaches (∼48 pp higher precision, and ∼29 pp higher recall) and deep learning based approaches (on average ∼44 pp higher precision and ∼60 pp higher recall) (Figure 3).

Snippet: The notion of complacency is mentioned frequently in the aviation human factors literature [61] and the term has long been absorbed into the vernacular of aviation accident reports [62], [63] as a causal factor. In a survey of leading airline captains [64], more than half thought that complacency was the leading cause of aviation accidents. The notion is considered by some as controversial. It is criticized, along with other concepts such as SA, mental workload, and trust as "folk" models in [35] with little underlying scientific basis and more common sense appeal. A counter-argument is given in [65] supporting these notions with an extensive data-base of empirical evidences, computational models and psychological foundations supporting SA, mental workload and trust. 

Wiener in [64] discussed complacency as a low level of suspicion but suggested more empirical research to understand any underlying mechanisms behind complacency. In [66], complacency is a term used to explain the higher rate of mis-detections of automation failure when the reliability of automation is increased. While there is no consensus on the exact definition of complacency, it is suggested in [67] that a working definition could be derived from the features of complacency common to both aviation accidental analyses and human performance studies. This set of features include human monitoring of automation, a sub-optimal frequency of monitoring of the automation [68], and finally observable degradation in system performance due to the sub-optimal monitoring. A conceptual model of complacency is given [67]. In this model, complacency is a dynamic variable that varies overtime through interactions with the automation, and affects the attention allocation of the operator, which in turns may or may not lead to errors in the operation of machines. 

Vigilance can be interpreted as the lack of complacency [66]. The notion of vigilance is usually defined in the human factors literature as the ability of the human operator to focus attention on a signal source for extended period of time while remaining alert to a particular signal [69]. The study of vigilance started with Mackworth's work in World War 2 to understand why sonar operators miss certain weak signals indicating the presence of submarines at the end of their watch.

Title: Enabling Civil Single-Pilot Operations: A State-of-the-Art Review
Snippet: Brown et al. [53] conducted a 3 decades review, investigating the lessons learned about the impact of automation on Human Factor in aviation. A valuable approach for this would also be the reconstruction of accidents, as these often provide scenarios that reveal both the advancements and potential challenges associated with automation. Within the manuscript, Brown analyzed a recent accident with the aim of identifying the potential contributing factors with a practical example. 

Complacency is described as the failure to be vigilant in supervising automation prior to the automation failure. Wickens et al. [55] report automation complacency as a possible cause of the attentional tunneling phenomenon. On the other hand, the out-of-the-loop syndrome occurs when users fail to continuously recognize what the automation is doing or not, often by excessively focusing on instrumentation and neglecting their physical surroundings. Most automation systems also suffer from brittleness, as described in the work of Christoffersen et al. [60]. In other words, a system's performance may be good for the range of situations for which it was designed, but it requires human intervention to handle situations outside those environments. Other issues deal with cultural considerations, especially concerning the way authority gradient in the cockpit modify when considering the automation as an additional member of the crew. According to the survey by Parasuraman [61], operators should try to avoid what are recognized as "misuse" and "disuse" scenarios, as well as the complete abuse of the automated systems' capabilities. A possible cognitive overhead in managing an automated subsystem could, in fact, even outweigh its potential benefits, so much to make it less attractive. 

As often acknowledged by industry insiders, technology challenges are not the primary obstacles for the practical implementation of single-pilot operations to date. Rather than simply automating a function, current designers should focus on determining the extent to which to do so, understanding when and why an aid should be used and the conditions under which it might be left unused. Some research around the topic of managing different automation control modes was already addressed by Kirlik [56], who analyzed some possible optimal policies for using the autopilot in both single and dual-crew conditions.

Title: Transport safety and human factors in the era of automation: What can transport modes learn from each other?
Snippet: Relevant examples from flight simulator research (Bailey and Scerbo, 2007) found a correlation between high levels of trust of the pilot and low levels of monitoring. This research was based on two studies which evaluated the impact of monitoring complexity, system reliability, operator trust and system experience on automation-induced complacency. 

Another study (Wickens et al., 1999) used a simulator to represent air-to ground targeting missions of 3 min, expecting guidance from a navigation system on a forward view. There was no cue on the 33 % of the simulation trials. On the 67 % of the cuing, 40 % were wrong. Pilots got directions to say 'target' and to focus their simulated aircraft boresight on the main objective and restraint the trigger when their purpose was right. They also got instructions to say 'abort' if they did not trust that the objective was in scene. After each trial, pilots were requested to express their decision confidence on a 4-point scale. The results were unexpected and demonstrated the risks of over-trust especially when automation supports difficult tasks for the user. Dorneich et al. (2017) did an empirical investigation which appraised key human factors issues associated with automation visibility and information quality. One test examined the interaction between automation visibility and information quality in the context of a decision-aiding automation. In this investigation, over-trust in the automation's recommendations led to failure to annul insignificant diversion aid instructions. Confidence did not change despite the different conditions. However, it had a negative result on the performance when information quality was low. Pilots spent less time checking for missing information due to their high trust in automation. 

Based on reports from the Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS), the variety of situation awareness errors in aviation was studied (Jones and Endsley, 1996). 143 episodes were studied, such as elements related to the failure of overseeing data by pilots and controllers, comprising overreliance on automation (2.77 % of the situation awareness errors). A greater number of the dependence on automation errors aroused from the expectation of the flight crew from the autopilot or the flight management system to perform significant tasks.

Title: Investigation on the impact of human-automation interaction in maritime operations
Snippet: In parallel to conducting this small scale experiment, some case studies from major aviation accidents that have strong links to automation shortcomings, were reviewed and key findings and learning outcomes were identified. In this review, there were examples of complex interactions between technical and human performance weaknesses, which led to a situation from which recovery was not possible. Automation limitations such as poor situation awareness, delegated authority and ineffective monitoring were identified in the aviation accident cases reviewed (NTSB, 2014). 

In the small scale experiment, the level of automation failure recognition was considered as poor. Half of the test subjects failed to effectively monitor the vessel's progress under the autopilot, and when questioned had incorrect situation awareness. 

After the earlier videos, where the automated systems function normally, a level of trust was established. 

Therefore, a degree of complacency may have been present. This complacency may explain why, for some Age group returning to complete the questionnaire. Greater weight was attributed to the information provided electronically and therefore the subtle turn of the vessel, and associated visual clues, went unnoticed.

documents.snippet:
Brown et al. [53] conducted a 3 decades review, investigating the lessons learned about the impact of automation on Human Factor in aviation. A valuable approach for this would also be the reconstruction of accidents, as these often provide scenarios that reveal both the advancements and potential challenges associated with automation. Within the manuscript, Brown analyzed a recent accident with the aim of identifying the potential contributing factors with a practical example. 

Complacency is described as the failure to be vigilant in supervising automation prior to the automation failure. Wickens et al. [55] report automation complacency as a possible cause of the attentional tunneling phenomenon. On the other hand, the out-of-the-loop syndrome occurs when users fail to continuously recognize what the automation is doing or not, often by excessively focusing on instrumentation and neglecting their physical surroundings. Most automation systems also suffer from brittleness, as described in the work of Christoffersen et al. [60]. In other words, a system's performance may be good for the range of situations for which it was designed, but it requires human intervention to handle situations outside those environments. Other issues deal with cultural considerations, especially concerning the way authority gradient in the cockpit modify when considering the automation as an additional member of the crew. According to the survey by Parasuraman [61], operators should try to avoid what are recognized as "misuse" and "disuse" scenarios, as well as the complete abuse of the automated systems' capabilities. A possible cognitive overhead in managing an automated subsystem could, in fact, even outweigh its potential benefits, so much to make it less attractive. 

As often acknowledged by industry insiders, technology challenges are not the primary obstacles for the practical implementation of single-pilot operations to date. Rather than simply automating a function, current designers should focus on determining the extent to which to do so, understanding when and why an aid should be used and the conditions under which it might be left unused. Some research around the topic of managing different automation control modes was already addressed by Kirlik [56], who analyzed some possible optimal policies for using the autopilot in both single and dual-crew conditions.

Relevant examples from flight simulator research (Bailey and Scerbo, 2007) found a correlation between high levels of trust of the pilot and low levels of monitoring. This research was based on two studies which evaluated the impact of monitoring complexity, system reliability, operator trust and system experience on automation-induced complacency. 

Another study (Wickens et al., 1999) used a simulator to represent air-to ground targeting missions of 3 min, expecting guidance from a navigation system on a forward view. There was no cue on the 33 % of the simulation trials. On the 67 % of the cuing, 40 % were wrong. Pilots got directions to say 'target' and to focus their simulated aircraft boresight on the main objective and restraint the trigger when their purpose was right. They also got instructions to say 'abort' if they did not trust that the objective was in scene. After each trial, pilots were requested to express their decision confidence on a 4-point scale. The results were unexpected and demonstrated the risks of over-trust especially when automation supports difficult tasks for the user. Dorneich et al. (2017) did an empirical investigation which appraised key human factors issues associated with automation visibility and information quality. One test examined the interaction between automation visibility and information quality in the context of a decision-aiding automation. In this investigation, over-trust in the automation's recommendations led to failure to annul insignificant diversion aid instructions. Confidence did not change despite the different conditions. However, it had a negative result on the performance when information quality was low. Pilots spent less time checking for missing information due to their high trust in automation. 

Based on reports from the Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS), the variety of situation awareness errors in aviation was studied (Jones and Endsley, 1996). 143 episodes were studied, such as elements related to the failure of overseeing data by pilots and controllers, comprising overreliance on automation (2.77 % of the situation awareness errors). Below are aviation AI challenges that recent surveys, certification analyses, and sector reviews indicate are both critical and systematically underemphasized in the research literature. Each section links evidence that these issues are (a) growing operational constraints, (b) flagged as gaps by regulators/standards bodies, and (c) sparsely studied relative to technical feasibility.

Certification and safety assurance for evolving/learning AI
- Aviation regulators have articulated risk-based pathways for AI assurance, yet core certification gaps remain open: robust methods for evolving/learning AI, bias mitigation, and comprehensive guidelines for autonomous systems are still lacking, with ethical oversight receiving minimal focus in practice <cite id="a7a54be1-0">Aviation regulators have begun to formalize strategies for safe AI integration via EASA’s AI Roadmap 2.0 and the FAA Roadmap for AI Safety Assurance, but these high-level documents highlight the need for standardized assurance and point to critical gaps in certification methods for evolving AI, bias mitigation, and regulatory guidance for autonomous systems</cite> <cite id="a7a54be1-3">Learning AI improves adaptability but introduces unpredictability, limited explainability, and bias risks that current safety methodologies struggle to address, with gaps including certification for evolving models, inadequate bias mitigation, and limited regulatory guidance</cite> <cite id="a7a54be1-2">There are major challenges in aviation AI regulation, including uncertainty in certification standards, difficulties applying XAI, and cybersecurity concerns in AI-based predictive maintenance</cite>. 
- These challenges are recognized not just as future hurdles but present obstacles to certification of current learning systems, with regulators noting the absence of a set path for fully autonomous flight and calling for coordinated development of safety cases and assurance processes <cite id="a7a54be1-0">Artificial Intelligence is disrupting aviation; regulators such as the FAA and EASA currently have no set path to certification for fully autonomous flying aircraft, though both agencies are working to formalize strategies for safe integration</cite>. 
- EASA’s concept paper explicitly lists three guarantees needed before certification: ML model generalization, data completeness/representativeness, and model robustness—areas where research and operational practice are still immature relative to the regulatory push <cite id="a7a54be1-4">EASA identifies three objectives for AI/ML certification requiring further research: guarantees on ML model generalization, guarantees on data completeness and representativeness, and guarantees on model robustness</cite>.

Explainability, transparency, and maintainable human oversight
- Despite technical progress, research repeatedly calls out explainability as a bottleneck for trust among regulators and operators and for enabling consistent safety assurance as AI systems learn and evolve <cite id="ac5d3b05-0">Improving AI transparency and explainability is crucial to build trust among regulators and operators; further research is needed to ensure consistent safety assurance as AI systems learn and evolve</cite> <cite id="ac5d3b05-2">AI systems in aviation require transparency for accountability and ethical concerns, especially in high-stakes environments where decisions affect life-and-death outcomes</cite>. 
- Human-in-the-loop integration is a persistent challenge: maintaining pilot situational awareness in increasingly automated cockpits and ensuring appropriate human–AI collaboration models are not yet mature and are not matched by sufficient empirical study <cite id="ac5d3b05-0">Integrating autonomous systems with existing air traffic management and ensuring pilots remain situationally aware in increasingly automated cockpits are ongoing hurdles</cite> <cite id="ac5d3b05-1">Research into XAI and computer-aided verification needs to keep pace with applied AI to close gaps that would hinder operational deployment of higher levels of automation in ATM</cite>. 
- Surveyed work emphasizes that the current body of research spans human–AI teaming and regulation, but cognitive integration and oversight remain thin relative to algorithmic performance metrics <cite id="ac5d3b05-3">Existing research covers technical applications and human-centered issues, yet systematic literature review shows gaps that require further work on human–AI teaming, cognitive integration, and regulation, certification, and safety assurance to build legitimacy and trust</cite>.

Data coverage, domain shift, and representativeness
- Certification roadmaps explicitly require guarantees of model generalization and data completeness/representativeness, yet the literature consistently notes that real-world operational data are insufficiently diverse and curated for robust deployment across spatio-temporal scales of aviation operations <cite id="a7a54be1-4">EASA’s certification objectives highlight guarantees on ML model generalization and on data completeness and representativeness as areas requiring further research</cite>. 
- Research syntheses repeatedly call out bias, data integrity, and cybersecurity as risks that must be managed with existing methods and more work to ensure consistent safety assurance as AI learns/evolves, underscoring that these are not adequately addressed in many applied studies <cite id="ac5d3b05-0">Concerns about data integrity, bias, and cybersecurity pose risks that must be carefully managed; further research is needed to ensure consistent safety assurance as AI systems learn and evolve</cite> <cite id="a7a54be1-2">Regulatory assessments identify uncertainty in standards, XAI difficulties, and cybersecurity concerns as major challenges for AI in aviation</cite>.

Robustness, adversarial threats, and cyber-physical resilience
- GNSS spoofing and interference are recognized as significant threats to navigation, yet AI-based detection tailored to civilian aviation remains relatively limited, with calls for more aviation-specific ML research, larger operational datasets, and real-time architectures validated in situ <cite id="6dcfded1-1">Despite growing interest in AI-driven cybersecurity, research on AI-based GNSS spoofing detection in aviation environments remains relatively limited, creating the need for further investigation into AI techniques tailored to civilian aviation applications</cite> <cite id="6dcfded1-2">Few studies have applied machine learning specifically to aviation GNSS spoofing and interference, indicating the need for additional research to assess AI effectiveness in this domain</cite> <cite id="6dcfded1-0">Recommendations include incorporating anomaly detection with multi-layered signal authentication and encouraging R&D on GNSS cybersecurity; more realistic validation with large datasets and operational environments is needed</cite>. 
- Broader cybersecurity reviews find spoofing, jamming, DoS, and malware remain prevalent threats, yet ML-based mitigation/validation lacks standardization and rigorous operational verification, pointing to a gap between promising techniques and dependable assurance in ATM/aircraft systems <cite id="6dcfded1-4">A review of 10 peer-reviewed studies across aircraft systems, ATM, airport infrastructure, and UAVs found spoofing, jamming, DoS, and malware are common threats; ML-based detection/mitigation and encryption are suggested, but validation remains intangible, necessitating standardization frameworks and unity across technology, operations, and policy</cite>.

Human factors and cognitive ergonomics at scale (ATM/airspace and operations)
- Moving from off-wing applications to in-wing and in-airspace autonomy, cognitive ergonomics, workload, trust, and role allocation are not yet empirically grounded at national/sector scale; cognitive tasks are increasingly supported by AI, but adaptive collaboration and oversight models require sustained research to prevent degrading situational awareness or decision quality <cite id="ac5d3b05-3">Research on human–AI teaming and cognitive integration shows AI augments performance and redistributes workload, with implications for trust, role allocation, and adaptive collaboration</cite> <cite id="ac5d3b05-0">Ensuring pilots remain situationally aware in increasingly automated cockpits is an ongoing hurdle as autonomous systems integrate with existing air traffic management</cite>. 
- ATM modernization and UTM introduce new socio-technical constraints: vendor verification, regulatory certification, and end-user acceptance must be addressed together, yet XAI and computer-aided verification lags applied AI deployments, creating a bottleneck for operationalization <cite id="ac5d3b05-1">Applied AI in ATM raises requirements for vendor verification, regulatory certification, and end-user acceptance; research into XAI and computer-aided verification must close gaps to enable deployment</cite>. 
- Surveyed work underscores that regulation, certification, and safety assurance—key to legitimate deployment—are underdeveloped relative to the breadth of technical applications being prototyped, with calls for adaptive certification frameworks and transparent oversight <cite id="ac5d3b05-3">Regulation, certification, and safety assurance have emerged as critical domains, with the need for adaptive frameworks, transparent oversight, and proactive governance to build legitimacy and public trust</cite>.

Ethics, bias, public trust, and global harmonization
- Ethical considerations and bias mitigation are repeatedly cited as weak points in current assurance toolkits and in regulatory guidance, with public trust hinging on accountable, transparent AI; these areas receive minimal focus in many applied studies despite their centrality to societal acceptance <cite id="a7a54be1-3">Ethical considerations receive minimal focus, indicating an area requiring further exploration to ensure safe, reliable AI integration and accountability</cite> <cite id="ac5d3b05-0">AI transparency and explainability are crucial to build trust among regulators and operators, and consistent safety assurance as AI learns and evolves remains an open area</cite>. 
- Harmonization across regulators (EU AI Act risk-based approach vs. US industry consensus) creates uncertainty and impedes global assurance, yet little research directly measures the impact of this fragmentation on safety assurance, certification timelines, and innovation trajectories in aviation AI <cite id="a7a54be1-2">Disharmony between EASA’s EASA AI Act and the FAA’s industry consensus-based approach poses a major challenge for globally applicable certification standards, with uncertainty in certification, difficulties in XAI, and cybersecurity concerns</cite>.

Why these are “systematically underestimated”
- Regulator roadmaps acknowledge risk-based certification but leave evolving/learning AI, bias, and ethics under-specified; agencies call for coordinated standards and robust methods yet point to persistent gaps, indicating the research community has not yet built commensurate assurance toolchains and evidence bases <cite id="a7a54be1-0">High-level FAA and EASA roadmaps provide pathways for AI safety assurance but emphasize the need for standardized assurance and highlight certification gaps for evolving AI</cite> <cite id="a7a54be1-3">Lack of robust certification methods for evolving AI, inadequate bias mitigation, and absence of comprehensive regulatory guidelines are explicit gaps</cite>. 
- Operational realities (GNSS spoofing, cyber-physical threats) are well-documented, yet peer-reviewed, aviation-specific ML-based defenses with in-situ validation are sparse; reviews stress that ML-based mitigations remain unvalidated at scale and that standardization is lacking, pointing to a systematic underinvestment relative to threat salience <cite id="6dcfded1-1">Aviation-specific AI-based GNSS spoofing detection is relatively limited, necessitating further investigation</cite> <cite id="6dcfded1-4">ML-based detection/mitigation validation remains intangible and requires standardization frameworks</cite>. 
- Human factors research often emphasizes workload/trust qualitatively, but there is insufficient quantitative evidence on how adaptive collaboration degrades or preserves situational awareness and decision quality as autonomy levels increase across ATM/airspace and mixed-traffic operations <cite id="ac5d3b05-3">Studies show AI redistributes workload and transforms teamwork, but systematic evidence for adaptive collaboration and oversight under high automation remains limited</cite> <cite id="ac5d3b05-0">Maintaining pilot situational awareness is an ongoing hurdle in increasingly automated cockpits</cite>. 
- Data coverage and domain shift are formalized as certification objectives, yet many studies benchmark on curated or geographically narrow datasets; literature calls for guarantees of representativeness and robustness point to an underemphasis on spatio-temporal coverage, rare edge cases, and continuous learning governance in aviation contexts <cite id="a7a54be1-4">Guarantees on model generalization and data completeness/representativeness are explicitly required and still require further research</cite> <cite id="ac5d3b05-0">Research is needed to ensure consistent safety assurance as AI systems learn and evolve, with data integrity and bias as key concerns</cite>.

Practical directions to address underestimation
- Build aviation-specific, adversarially aware ML pipelines validated in situ with GNSS and navigation redundancy, and develop multi-layered authentication schemes integrated with anomaly detection and real-time verification loops <cite id="6dcfded1-0">Anomaly detection with multi-layered signal authentication and real-time AI-based monitoring architectures are recommended, with calls for larger operational datasets and realistic tests</cite> <cite id="6dcfded1-4">Standardization frameworks and unity across technology, operations, and policy are needed to achieve resilience</cite>. 
- Co-develop certification-by-design frameworks with regulators: W-shaped learning assurance processes, bias audits, and maintainable safety cases that evolve with models; prioritize explainability targets that are verifiable by oversight bodies and transparent to operators <cite id="a7a54be1-4">EASA’s W-shaped learning assurance process supersedes the non-AI V-cycle and emphasizes explainability and safety risk mitigation</cite> <cite id="a7a54be1-1">EASA and FAA guidelines frame trustworthiness analysis, assurance, human factors, and risk mitigation, but industry-academia cooperation is urgently needed to align massive AI methods with certification cycles</cite>. 
- Advance human–AI teaming research with controlled field studies in ATM and operations to quantify effects of automation on situational awareness, role allocation, and decision quality; integrate XAI and verification into applied ATM/UTM evaluations to close deployment gaps <cite id="ac5d3b05-1">Applied AI in ATM requires XAI and computer-aided verification to close deployment gaps and accommodate ground-based ATM into certification frameworks</cite> <cite id="ac5d3b05-3">Human–AI teaming and cognitive integration research must deepen to address adaptive collaboration and oversight under high automation</cite>. 
- Establish global harmonization of ethics, bias, and cybersecurity audits for aviation AI; align EU and US approaches to reduce uncertainty and accelerate credible assurance for cross-border operations and UAM/UTM integration <cite id="a7a54be1-2">Regional differences (EASA AI Act vs. FAA industry consensus) create certification uncertainty; ethical considerations, XAI difficulties, and cybersecurity concerns are prominent challenges</cite>.

Summary
Across certification, human factors, robustness, data, and governance, the literature consistently flags gaps that mirror real-world constraints in aviation. These challenge areas are not only technically difficult but also socio-technical and regulatory, where assurance must keep pace with innovation. The systematic underestimation manifests as a mismatch between the volume of algorithmic papers and the maturity of safety cases, explainability for oversight, robustness to adversarial conditions, and human-centered integration at scale. Addressing this mismatch will require coordinated regulator–industry research agendas, aviation-specific datasets and validation environments, and human–AI teaming studies that deliver quantifiable gains in safety and situational awareness as autonomy increases <cite id="ac5d3b05-0">Certification challenges persist due to the probabilistic nature of AI; data integrity, bias, cybersecurity, and integration with air traffic management are ongoing hurdles</cite> <cite id="ac5d3b05-1">XAI and computer-aided verification must keep pace to close gaps hindering operational deployment in ATM</cite> <cite id="a7a54be1-3">Lack of robust methods for evolving AI, inadequate bias mitigation, and minimal ethical focus are explicit gaps needing further exploration</cite> <cite id="6dcfded1-1">Aviation-specific AI-based GNSS spoofing detection remains relatively limited, underscoring underexplored robustness challenges</cite> <cite id="a7a54be1-4">Guarantees on model generalization, data completeness/representativeness, and robustness are listed as prerequisites for certification and still require further research</cite>.
